title: What was Instagram earning?
lede: Facebook agreed to pay about US$1 billion for Instagram in April 2012. Before you look it up, decide how much revenue you think Instagram was making.
intent: Learners can explain what an acquirer is buying when it pays for a company with no revenue.
goal: explain what a buyer is paying for when a company has no revenue at all.
question: When Facebook agreed to pay about US$1 billion for Instagram, how much revenue was Instagram making?

options.label: Nothing at all
options.feedback: Right. Instagram had never charged anyone for anything, and ran no advertising.

options.label: About US$10 million a year
options.feedback: A reasonable guess for a popular app, but Instagram had no revenue at all.

options.label: About US$100 million a year
options.feedback: That would put the price at ten times revenue, a common rule of thumb. The real answer makes the rule of thumb useless.

options.label: About US$1 billion a year
options.feedback: That would make the deal look cheap. In fact Instagram earned nothing.

reveal.heading: Nothing. So what was Facebook buying?
reveal.explanation: Instagram had no revenue, no advertising and thirteen staff. What Facebook paid for was about 30 million users, a team that had built something people used every day, and the certainty that a competitor would not own it.
points: When a company has no revenue, its price is a bet about the future, not a calculation about the present.
Buying a company partly to stop a rival buying it is a strategy with a name: a defensive acquisition.

stats.label: Employees at the time of sale
Revenue at the time of sale
Registered users at the time
stats.detail: Registered accounts, not monthly active users.

teach.watchFor: The "$0" landing as a joke. Stay with it: ask the room to list what, apart from revenue, could be worth a billion dollars.
ask: What else, apart from revenue, could be worth paying for?
